title: What inspired means
hook: all-scripture-is-God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16) is read by some as word-for-word, by others as God working through human writers

segments.voice: Yesterday, how the Bible was gathered: letters read aloud in worship until the churches knew which books were theirs. Your line was the church read these.

Dust, shaped into a person, lying still on the ground. Not alive yet. Then, in the second chapter of Genesis, God leans close: "and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Dust, plus breath, equals someone. Hold that picture, because a short line in a letter that opens with Paul's name reaches for the same breath, and Christians read it in more than one way. Today's word: inspiration.

The word inspiration carries a picture of breath. The line is in the second letter to Timothy: "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness." Behind the King James phrase is a Greek word, theopneustos, usually rendered God-breathed. Genesis again: God breathes, and something lifeless comes alive. Notice what the verse spends its breath on. It doesn't explain how the breathing worked. It says what scripture is for: teaching, correcting, setting straight, training. It's written to Timothy, who, it says, has known the holy scriptures from a child. It's practical. The how is where Christians read differently. Some, often evangelical, stress that God guided the writers so closely that the very words are what God intended, and teach that the Bible is without error in all it affirms. Others put the weight on God working through human writers: their languages, styles, times and personalities. Catholic teaching holds the two together: God is the author of scripture, the human writers are true authors too, and the books teach without error the truth God wanted written down for our salvation. Orthodox and Protestant teachers stand at different points along that line. Both sides lean on a verse in the second letter of Peter: "holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost." Divine and human in the same sentence. Christians argue about how much weight each half carries. They agree on the breath: a book that, they say, didn't just get written. It got breathed into.

Breathe in, and on the out-breath say quietly: all scripture is given by inspiration of God. On the next out-breath: and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness. Then just breathe, noticing that every word rode out on air; if you pray, ask that the words you read be alive for you, and if not, simply rest in the breath.
Inspiration. A breath word. In 2 Timothy, scripture is God-breathed, and useful for teaching and training.
Your line: god-breathed. Dust, and then breath, and then someone comes alive. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians call the Bible inspired, God-breathed; some, often evangelical, stress that its very words are without error, others stress God working through true human authors, and Catholic teaching affirms both.

chat.says: When Christians call the Bible inspired, do they mean the writers just felt inspired?
options: More than that: 2 Timothy calls scripture God-breathed, though churches differ on how it worked.
It means every church agrees the verse explains exactly how God guided each writer.
It means only the Gospels count, since the verse is about Jesus's own spoken words.
chat.meaning: In 2 Timothy, scripture is God-breathed. The verse says what scripture is for, not how; Christians differ on how God and the human writers worked.

notes: 'Inspiration means breathing in' is the plain sense of the English/Latin word (inspirare); flagged under the claims rule as an etymology. 'Theopneustos, usually rendered God-breathed' is attributed. Confirm.

Inerrancy described as held by 'some Christians, often evangelical', 'without error in all it affirms' (Chicago Statement wording, paraphrased). Catholic teaching (Dei Verbum 11: God as author, the human writers as true authors) paraphrased. Orthodox grouped with 'God working through human writers'; check the Orthodox placement is fair.
The letter is called 'one of Paul's letters' in the hook, following its opening (2 Timothy 1:1); authorship is debated by scholars. Consider 'a letter in Paul's name'.

Audit: 'clay' changed to 'dust' (Genesis 2:7 says dust of the ground); teach, howItsDone, myth and trapdoor no longer set Catholic teaching against inerrancy (Dei Verbum 11 affirms both true human authors and that the books teach without error the truth God willed for our salvation), and evangelical teaching is no longer framed as denying human authorship. Orthodox placement kept general.
